title: Fear Conditioning
subtitle: Learning that cues predict danger
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating fear conditioning across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain fear conditioning in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in fear conditioning.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to fear conditioning.

sections.explainSimply: Fear conditioning links previously neutral cues with aversive outcomes.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Generalisation can spread responding to safe cues that resemble the original threat, while avoidance prevents corrective learning.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Human trauma involves language, meaning and social context beyond laboratory conditioning, so conditioning models are informative but incomplete.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of fear conditioning as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need fear conditioning to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Conditioning is not a complete explanation of PTSD.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use fear conditioning to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses fear conditioning to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Conditioning is not a complete explanation of PTSD. Evidence classification: established learning mechanism.
